antiPatterns: Repeatedly attempting the same density-dependent culling mechanism that has failed in the last three cycles.
Focusing on fox reproductive traits that don't account for energy scarcity.

directions.avoid: Traits that increase fox metabolic efficiency or stress resilience.
directions.label: A
directions.title: Indirect Fox Reproductive Constraint
directions.why: Direct density-dependent culling and simple reproductive caps have failed. Target fox reproductive resilience specifically when individuals are under metabolic stress/starvation.

directions.avoid: Mechanisms that dump the entire buffer at once without consumption capacity.
directions.expectedGardenEffect: Reduction in nutrient buffer and further increase in active nutrients.
directions.label: B
directions.title: Optimize Nutrient Buffer Release
directions.why: Active nutrients have improved, but the 100-unit nutrient buffer remains locked, indicating a failure to convert stored energy effectively.

directions.avoid: Mechanisms that only benefit higher-trophic-level organisms.
directions.label: C
directions.title: Enhance Fungal-Root Synergy
directions.why: Foundational organisms are successfully growing; further synergy will make them more competitive for energy against foxes.

directions.avoid: Traits that focus on beetle reproduction at the cost of survival against predators.
directions.expectedGardenEffect: Stable growth of the beetle population.
directions.label: D
directions.title: Sustain Beetle Growth
directions.why: The beetle population is thriving but remains vulnerable. Maintain current gains.

results.evidence: Active nutrients increased from 9 to 61, but the nutrient buffer remains stuck at 100.
results.label: B

review.summary: Beetle and foundational organism growth were successful, but direct fox control attempts remain inert, and the nutrient buffer remains stagnant despite active nutrient improvements.

thesis: The ecosystem is thriving in beetle and fungal counts but remains structurally imbalanced due to an excessively high and unresponsive fox population. With beetle recovery secured, the immediate priority is to break the fox's dominance of the energy cycle. Previous attempts to cap the fox population have been inert; we must now shift strategies to either directly constrain fox reproductive resilience or shift resource allocation so aggressively toward foundational organisms (fungus/root network) that the fox population declines due to natural resource competition and scarcity.
